headline: Captree dock talk: the bunker showed up right on schedule, and so did the blues
subhead: Fire Island Inlet is loading up with peanut bunker and mullet, blitz activity is building, and the fluke bite is starting to thin out as fall takes hold.
body_markdown:
There was a mate leaning on the rail at the Captree docks Sunday morning, coffee in hand, telling anyone who'd listen that he watched three separate bird balls working off Democrat Point before the sun was even fully up. That's the kind of report that gets repeated dock to dock all day, and by noon half the fleet had heard some version of it. We flagged this last week — said the blitz activity would build as the tide range strengthened and bait got squeezed tight against the beach — and here it is, right on time.

The mullet and peanut bunker run is properly underway along the barrier beach now, funneling through Fire Island Inlet on the moving tide and stacking up wherever there's a current seam to hold them. That's pulling bluefish in behind the bait in real numbers, and the stripers are starting to shadow those pods tighter than they have all summer. It's not a blind blitz yet where you can just run and gun all day, but the windows are real — first light and the last two hours of the ebb have been the money stretches at Democrat Point and along the ocean side of Robert Moses field 2.

A lot of that has to do with what's happening offshore versus inside. The ocean's been carrying some size — buoy readings off the Bight have shown better than 3-foot swell on a short period, which makes the open beachfront sloppy and inconsistent for wading anglers. That rough water is actually working in the bay's favor: it's pushing bait and predators into the stable, structured water inside the inlet rather than letting them spread out along the open coast. If you've been getting bounced around trying to fish the exposed ocean beach, shift your effort to the inlet channels and the flats just inside — that's where the fish have been concentrating.

On the striper side, the pattern is still building rather than roaring. Guys working bucktails — 1 to 1.5-ounce white or bone colored, tipped with a strip of fresh bunker — along the deep edge of the Democrat Point rip have been picking at slot fish on the last of the outgoing, working the current seam where the clean green water meets the darker push coming out of the bay. Live-lining bunker on a fish-finder rig off Robert Moses field 5 and the west end of Fire Island has also produced, though it's still more a pick than a blitz most mornings. Give it another week or two of cooling water and building bait pressure and this typically turns into the real event — that's the pattern every fall, and there's no reason to think this year breaks from it.

Bluefish are the more reliable bite right now. Chopper blues in the 4 to 8-pound class have been mixed into those bird-working schools off the inlet, and they're not shy — bucktails, metal (Deadly Dicks and Hopkins in silver), and topwater plugs worked fast through the bait balls have all drawn strikes. The bite tends to shut off almost as fast as it opens once the birds settle, so when you see working birds off the inlet or along the beach at Cedar Beach, it pays to run to it rather than wait it out.

Fluke is the one that's fading, and it's fading right on schedule. The Robert Moses bridges and the deeper holes off Oak Beach have still been giving up keeper fluke to 4 and 5 pounds on white Gulp Swimming Mullets and chartreuse bucktails, fished slow on the drift in 25 to 35 feet, but the counts are down from where they were in August. Fish are starting their exit toward deeper ocean water as the bay cools, and that exodus typically accelerates hard through the rest of September. If fluke is the target, don't wait — the next two weeks are probably what's left of it before the bite tapers to almost nothing inside.

Porgies have been a quiet, steady producer in the bay for anyone who wants an easier day — small pieces of clam or squid on a hi-lo rig around the Patchogue and Sayville flats, working the deeper holes on the last of the tide, has kept rods bent for anyone who isn't chasing the blitz. Blackfish season is starting to get talked about at the dock as water eases, though it's early yet — worth keeping an eye on structure around the inlet jetties as fall deepens. Weakfish have been mostly absent from the conversation this week; if they're around, nobody's talking about it yet.

Looking ahead, the next few days should keep building on this pattern. The tide range is still increasing toward the upcoming moon, which means stronger current at the inlet and more bait getting pinned against structure — that's exactly the recipe that turns a pick-and-peck bass bite into something with teeth. If there's only one window to fish this week, make it the last two hours of the ebb at Democrat Point or off Robert Moses field 5, right as the bait gets squeezed and the birds start working. Keep an eye on the ocean swell, too — if it lays down even a little, the exposed beachfront could turn on fast as bass push up tight to the sandbars chasing mullet.
